parts.label: (a)
parts.text: State the reason why two objects that are at the same temperature are described as being in thermal equilibrium.

parts.label: (b)(i)
parts.stem:
Fig. 3.1 shows the variations with temperature of the densities of mercury and of water between $0^{\circ}\text{C}$ and $100^{\circ}\text{C}$.

{{figure:figure_3_1.png}}

Temperature may be measured using the variation with temperature of the density of a liquid.

Suggest why, for measuring temperature over this temperature range:

parts.label: (b)(ii)
parts.text: water is not a suitable liquid.

parts.label: (c)(i)
parts.text: State the boiling temperature, in $^{\circ}\text{C}$, of the liquid.

parts.label: (c)(ii)
parts.text: Determine the specific heat capacity, in $\text{J g}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1}$, of the liquid.

parts.label: (d)
parts.text:
The experiment in (c) is repeated using water instead of the liquid in (c). The mass of liquid used, the power supplied, and the initial temperature are all unchanged.
The specific heat capacity of water is approximately twice that of the liquid in (c).
The boiling temperature of water is $100^{\circ}\text{C}$.

On Fig. 3.2, sketch the variation with time $t$ of the temperature of the water between $t = 0$ and $t = 60\text{ s}$. Numerical calculations are not required.
